Its mere two horsehair strings limit the range, which lies mostly in the low middle register, warm in quality and a little coarse. It is played like a cello, but with so few strings the resonance is simple and direct: it lacks the bright penetration of the violin, yet it resonates more deeply. Compared with bowed instruments of its own time the gue is more inward and quiet, sitting between the heaviness of the cello and the plainness of a folk string instrument. Its sound has a strong flavour of Nordic folk music, coarse in quality and expressive, and it reflects the old musical culture of the Shetland Islands.

The gue is an extinct bowed chordophone of the Shetland Islands, of the two-string bowed lyre or zither type. An account of 1809 says that musicians played it before the fiddle arrived; it looked like a fiddle, had only two horsehair strings, and was bowed like a cello. Its exact construction is unknown; it may have been close to bowed lyres such as the Norwegian giga, the Swedish and Estonian talharpa and the Finnish jouhikko, or to two-string bowed zithers such as the Icelandic fiðla.

In 1809 Arthur Edmondston recorded that players used it before the violin was introduced; it had two horsehair strings and was played like a cello. Its form is unknown; it may resemble bowed lyres such as the Norwegian giga, the Swedish and Estonian talharpa and the Finnish jouhikko, and it is also thought close to the Icelandic fiðla. Peter Cooke, noting that the Canadian Inuit bowed instrument was popular in areas influenced by Orkney and Shetland sailors, suggested it may have Shetland roots. In 2007 Corwin Broch began a reconstruction, made one for the Shetland Museum in 2009, and in 2012 the design went onto a drawing disc, which became the basis for later builds.
